newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan says U.S. Congress cannot legislate for U.N..
newsitem.headline: Annan says U.S. Congress cannot legislate for U.N..

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Thursday the United States Congress could not legislate for the other 184 U.N. members, who might not accept Washington's conditions for paying back dues.

He was referring to a bill under which the United States would pay $819 million of its U.N. arrears over three years but would set a number of conditions or "benchmarks." The world body calculates the U.S. debt at $1.3 billion.

Annan told a news conference: "One can discuss these things in Congress. It does not mean that it is going to become law in the U.N. It does not necessarily mean that the member states are going to accept it.
"My sense is that quite a lot of the issues, the U.S. will have to come and negotiate and discuss with the other member states. It is going to be quite a challenge for U.S. diplomacy."
Annan said the U.S. administration realised this, "and I don't think anyone expects that Congress can take decisions and impose them unilaterally on the other 184 member states."
As a condition of the U.S. payment, the bill before the Republican-dominated Congress would demand a string of U.N. spending cuts, a reduction in U.S. annual dues and other concessions.

Noting the legislation was still being negotiated between the U.S. administration and Congress, Annan said he was very pleased with a speech by Senator Richard Lugar, a leading Republican senator, who pressed for U.S. fulfilment of its obligations.

Annan said: "The president himself is convinced that the U.N. is essential for the United States, just as we need the U.S. to participate actively in this organisation. He also believes that if the United States is going to lead and play an effective role in this organisation it has to pay its way."

The secretary-general said he was briefed by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and the State Department last week on the "very tough and delicate negotiations" between the administration and Congress. "They felt this was the best deal they could get under the circumstances and considered it a breakthrough and were happy with it."

Annan said he, like all the U.N. members, would have been "happier if the totality of what we believe is owed were paid and if the deck had been cleared, and that we did not have to deal with benchmarks," he added, referring to the conditions set by Congress.
